title: Baseline healthy application and telemetry
description: Project: Baseline healthy application and telemetry. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: Before you can detect incidents, you need to know what healthy looks like. This lesson establishes a baseline for the application: golden-signal metrics, structured logging, distributed tracing, and synthetic health checks. A well-instrumented baseline makes every later incident investigation faster because you can answer 'is this new?' in seconds instead of hours.

items: Golden signals collected per service: request rate, error rate, request duration, and saturation
Structured JSON logs with severity, service name, trace ID, and user context on every request
Distributed traces that cross API, database, and cache boundaries with consistent sampling
Synthetic health-check endpoints verified every ten seconds from outside the cluster
Alerting thresholds derived from SLOs, not arbitrary numbers, with runbook links attached
Dashboard panels that a new team member can read without asking for definitions

terms.definition: The four key metrics Google recommends for monitoring any service: traffic, errors, latency, and saturation.
Service Level Objective: a target reliability threshold, such as 99.9% successful requests over a rolling 30-day window.
The allowable number of failures before an SLO is breached; consumed by real incidents and refreshed on a fixed window.
Logs emitted as JSON objects with typed fields rather than free-form strings, enabling reliable filtering and correlation.
The practice of recording a fraction of traces to keep storage and compute costs manageable while preserving statistical significance.

items.text: Every HTTP endpoint emits a duration metric labeled by route and status code
items.hint: Use middleware or an AOT filter so instrumentation is unavoidable.

items.text: Every log line includes timestamp, severity, service, trace ID, and span ID
items.hint: Add a scoped logger that enriches context automatically.

items.text: Database queries are wrapped with timing and connection-count metrics
items.hint: EF Core interceptors and ADO.NET event listeners can emit these without touching business logic.

items.text: Health-check endpoints verify downstream dependencies, not just process uptime
items.hint: A check that returns 200 OK with a dead Redis instance is a false negative.

items.text: SLOs are documented in a runbook with breach procedures and escalation paths
items.hint: Runbooks reduce mean time to recovery by removing decision fatigue.

data.text: When you add instrumentation, instrument the critical path first. A payment API benefits more from a latency histogram than a marketing landing page. Start with the endpoints that directly affect revenue or safety, then expand outward. Also instrument failure paths. A system that only measures successes hides slow failures until users complain.

data.title: Avoid vanity metrics
data.text: Do not instrument what is easy to instrument. Instrument what helps you decide. A dashboard with 200 panels that no one reads is worse than three panels the on-call engineer consults during an incident. Audit dashboards quarterly and remove panels that have not been viewed in thirty days.

items.question: How many metrics should I collect per service?
items.answer: Start with the four golden signals plus saturation for each dependency. Add metrics only when you have a specific decision to make. More metrics mean more storage, more dashboard noise, and more alert fatigue.

items.question: Should I log every request or sample them?
items.answer: Log every request at a structured level if you have the storage budget. If volume is high, emit full logs for errors and sampled traces for successful requests, and keep the sampling rate tied to your error budget.

items.question: Who owns the telemetry pipeline?
items.answer: The platform or SRE team owns the pipeline and infrastructure, but each service team owns the instrumentation code inside their service. Shared ownership of dashboards without clear ownership of the underlying metrics leads to stale alerts.

data.title: Design a telemetry baseline
data.description: Pick a service you know well. List the golden signals you would instrument, the log fields you would add, and the three alerts you would create first. Explain why each metric matters and what decision it enables.
steps: Draw the service and its dependencies
Assign one metric to each dependency boundary
Define alert thresholds using SLO math, not guesswork
Write a one-paragraph runbook for each alert
data.expectedOutcome: You should produce a prioritized instrumentation plan that a team could implement in one sprint, with clear owners and success criteria.

data.title: Summary
points: Baseline instrumentation turns 'something feels off' into 'error rate spiked 3x in 2 minutes'
Golden signals give you a universal vocabulary across services
Structured logs with trace IDs connect metrics to traces to logs
Alert on decisions, not on numbers; every alert needs a runbook
Regularly audit and prune dashboards to prevent noise
data.takeaway: A senior engineer treats observability as a feature, not an afterthought. The time spent on baseline instrumentation pays back every time an incident occurs.
